proofs.proof_tex:
First, the restriction on \(c\) in the proposed statement is necessary.  By the definitions of \(\eta\) and \(\mathcal E_{\mathrm{loc}}\), the first coordinate of \(\eta\) is \(c\), whereas the first-coordinate projection of \(\operatorname{int}(\mathcal E_{\mathrm{loc}})\) is \((\underline c,\overline c)\).  Thus the frozen statement cannot hold when \(c=\underline c\) or \(c=\overline c\).

We now prove the corrected statement constructively.  Fix \(c\in(\underline c,\overline c)\) and a fixed \(r\).  Put
\[
 \mu^\circ=\frac{\underline\mu+\overline\mu}{2},
 \qquad
 v^\circ=\frac{\underline v+\overline v}{2}.
\]
The assumed strict inequalities \(0<\underline\mu<\overline\mu\) and \(0<\underline v<\overline v\) imply
\[
 \mu^\circ\in(\underline\mu,\overline\mu),
 \qquad
 v^\circ\in(\underline v,\overline v).
\]
For every sufficiently large integer \(k\), let
\[
 s_k=\lfloor ck\rfloor,\qquad T_k=4k,\qquad N_k=4s_k.
\]
Then \(N_k,T_k\to\infty\), and the definition \(c_N=N/T\) gives
\[
 c_{N_k}=\frac{N_k}{T_k}
 =\frac{s_k}{k}\longrightarrow c.
\]
Because \(c\) is strictly between the two aspect-ratio bounds, \(c_{N_k}\in(\underline c,\overline c)\) for all sufficiently large \(k\).

Suppress the index \(k\) on the arrays.  Define the support indicators by
\[
 d_i=\mathbf 1\{1\le i\le 2s_k\},
 \qquad
 qvec_t=\mathbf 1\{1\le t\le 2k\}.
\]
Consequently \(n_1=d^\top d=2s_k\), \(t_1=qvec^\top qvec=2k\), and hence
\[
 p_N=\frac{n_1}{N_k}=\frac12,
 \qquad
 q_T=\frac{t_1}{T_k}=\frac12.
\]
Define the score arrays by
\[
 a_i=
 \begin{cases}
 \mu^\circ+(-1)^i\sqrt{v^\circ},&1\le i\le 2s_k,\\
 0,&2s_k<i\le4s_k,
 \end{cases}
 \qquad
 b_t=
 \begin{cases}
 \mu^\circ+(-1)^t\sqrt{v^\circ},&1\le t\le 2k,\\
 0,&2k<t\le4k.
 \end{cases}
\]
Since \(a\) and \(b\) vanish off their respective supports, the definitions \(a_S=d\odot a\) and \(b_S=qvec\odot b\) give \(a_S=a\) and \(b_S=b\).  Each supported set has even cardinality, so it contains equally many plus and minus signs.  The definitions of the supported means therefore yield
\[
 \mu_{a,N}
 =\frac{1}{2s_k}\sum_{i=1}^{2s_k}
   \left(\mu^\circ+(-1)^i\sqrt{v^\circ}\right)
 =\mu^\circ,
 \qquad
 \mu_{b,T}
 =\frac{1}{2k}\sum_{t=1}^{2k}
   \left(\mu^\circ+(-1)^t\sqrt{v^\circ}\right)
 =\mu^\circ.
\]
After subtracting these means, every supported squared deviation equals \(v^\circ\).  The definitions of \(v_{a,N}\) and \(v_{b,T}\) thus give
\[
 v_{a,N}
 =\frac{1}{2s_k}\sum_{i=1}^{2s_k}v^\circ
 =v^\circ,
 \qquad
 v_{b,T}
 =\frac{1}{2k}\sum_{t=1}^{2k}v^\circ
 =v^\circ.
\]

Suppose first that \(r\ge1\), and let \(e_1,\ldots,e_r\) denote the standard basis of \(\mathbb R^r\).  Define
\[
 \rho(j)=1+((j-1)\bmod r).
\]
For all sufficiently large \(k\), \(2s_k\ge r\) and \(2k\ge r\).  Define the rows of the loading and factor matrices by
\[
 \Lambda_{i\cdot}=
 \begin{cases}
 0,&1\le i\le2s_k,\\
 e_{\rho(i-2s_k)}^\top,&2s_k<i\le4s_k,
 \end{cases}
 \qquad
 F_{t\cdot}=
 \begin{cases}
 0,&1\le t\le2k,\\
 e_{\rho(t-2k)}^\top,&2k<t\le4k.
 \end{cases}
\]
The nonzero rows of \(\Lambda\) occur only where \(d_i=0\), while \(a_S\) is zero there.  Hence, term by term,
\[
 \Lambda^\top d=\sum_{i=1}^{N_k}\Lambda_{i\cdot}^\top d_i=0,
 \qquad
 \Lambda^\top a_S=\sum_{i=1}^{N_k}\Lambda_{i\cdot}^\top(a_S)_i=0.
\]
Likewise, the nonzero rows of \(F\) occur only where \(qvec_t=0\), while \(b_S\) is zero there, and therefore
\[
 F^\top qvec=0,\qquad F^\top b_S=0.
\]

For \(\ell\in\{1,\ldots,r\}\), let
\[
 n_{\ell,k}=\#\{1\le j\le2s_k:\rho(j)=\ell\},
 \qquad
 f_{\ell,k}=\#\{1\le j\le2k:\rho(j)=\ell\}.
\]
The cyclic allocation implies
\[
 \left|n_{\ell,k}-\frac{2s_k}{r}\right|\le1,
 \qquad
 \left|f_{\ell,k}-\frac{2k}{r}\right|\le1.
\]
Direct multiplication of the displayed row definitions gives
\[
 \frac1{N_k}\Lambda^\top\Lambda
 =\operatorname{diag}\left(
   \frac{n_{1,k}}{4s_k},\ldots,\frac{n_{r,k}}{4s_k}
  \right)
 \longrightarrow \frac1{2r}I_r
\]
and
\[
 \frac1{T_k}F^\top F
 =\operatorname{diag}\left(
   \frac{f_{1,k}}{4k},\ldots,\frac{f_{r,k}}{4k}
  \right)
 \longrightarrow \frac1{2r}I_r.
\]
By the definitions of \(M_d\) and \(M_{qvec}\), the support placement gives \(M_d\Lambda=\Lambda\) and \(M_{qvec}F=F\).  Consequently
\[
 \frac1{N_k}\Lambda^\top M_d\Lambda
 =\frac1{N_k}\Lambda^\top\Lambda
 \longrightarrow\frac1{2r}I_r,
 \qquad
 \frac1{T_k}F^\top M_{qvec}F
 =\frac1{T_k}F^\top F
 \longrightarrow\frac1{2r}I_r.
\]
Both limits are positive definite.  Moreover, for all sufficiently large \(k\), every cyclic count is positive, so both \(\Lambda\) and \(F\) have column rank \(r\), and therefore \(\Lambda F^\top\) has rank \(r\).  If \(r=0\), take \(\Lambda\) and \(F\) to be the unique matrices with zero columns; all four orthogonality equalities hold and the Gram assertions are vacuous under the standard zero-dimensional convention.

Every row of \(\Lambda\) and \(F\) has Euclidean norm at most \(1\).  Also,
\[
 \max_i|a_i|\le\mu^\circ+\sqrt{v^\circ},
 \qquad
 \max_t|b_t|\le\mu^\circ+\sqrt{v^\circ}.
\]
Thus the loading, factor, and treatment-score rows are uniformly bounded in \(k\).

Collecting the calculations above,
\[
 \eta_{N_kT_k}
 =\left(c_{N_k},\frac12,\frac12,
         \mu^\circ,v^\circ,\mu^\circ,v^\circ\right)
 \longrightarrow
 \eta
 =\left(c,\frac12,\frac12,
         \mu^\circ,v^\circ,\mu^\circ,v^\circ\right).
\]
The condition \(\underline\pi\in(0,1/2)\) puts both share coordinates strictly inside \([\underline\pi,1-\underline\pi]\).  The strict inequalities already established for \(c,\mu^\circ,v^\circ\) put every other coordinate in the interior of its corresponding factor of \(\mathcal E_{\mathrm{loc}}\); in particular, each mean lies in the interior of the positive component \([\underline\mu,\overline\mu]\).  Hence \(\eta\in\operatorname{int}(\mathcal E_{\mathrm{loc}})\).

This construction uses only \(c,r\) and the fixed envelope constants.  It does not invoke \(\Phi_{\eta,h}\), \(h\), an argmin of \(\Phi_{\eta,h}\), or any selection from such an argmin.  It therefore supplies the asserted nonempty exact-oracle triangular-array class independently of any minimizer-selection rule.

proposed_statement_changes.proposed: For every fixed \(r\) and every \(c\in(\underline c,\overline c)\), there exist dimensions \(N,T\to\infty\) and deterministic arrays \(d,qvec,a,b,\Lambda,F\) such that \(c_N\to c\), \(\eta_{NT}\to\eta\in\operatorname{int}(\mathcal E_{\mathrm{loc}})\), \(\Lambda^{\top}d=\Lambda^{\top}a_S=0\), \(F^{\top}qvec=F^{\top}b_S=0\), the full Gram limits \(N^{-1}\Lambda^{\top}\Lambda\) and \(T^{-1}F^{\top}F\) are positive definite, the selector-restricted limits \(N^{-1}\Lambda^{\top}M_d\Lambda\) and \(T^{-1}F^{\top}M_{qvec}F\) are positive definite, and the loading, factor, and treatment-score rows are uniformly bounded. Hence the exact-oracle triangular-array class is nonempty without imposing any rule for selecting a minimizer of \(\Phi_{\eta,h}\).
proposed_statement_changes.reason: The frozen claim includes both endpoints of the aspect-ratio interval, but it simultaneously requires the limiting nuisance vector to lie in the ordinary interior of the product set. At either endpoint its first coordinate is on the boundary. Restricting the quantified aspect ratio to the open interval is therefore the minimal honest correction; every other conclusion is retained.

proofs.proof_tex:
Put \(U_0=\operatorname{col}(\Lambda)\) and \(V_0=\operatorname{col}(F)\).  The two Gram-envelope assumptions imply that these spaces have dimension \(r\) and that
\[
s_r\!\left(\frac{\Lambda F^{\top}}{\sigma\sqrt T}\right)
 \geq \frac{\sqrt{N\underline\lambda}\sqrt{T\underline f}}
 {\overline\sigma\sqrt T}
 \geq C_0\sqrt m                                             \tag{1}
\]
for \(C_0=\sqrt{\underline\lambda\underline f}/\overline\sigma>0\).  All remaining constants below can be chosen uniformly on a fixed compact subset of \(\mathcal G_{\mathrm{loc}}\).

The supported vectors admit the orthonormal decompositions
\[
e_1=\frac d{\sqrt{n_1}},\qquad
e_2=\frac{a_S-\mu_{a,N}d}{\sqrt{n_1v_{a,N}}},\qquad
f_1=\frac{qvec}{\sqrt{t_1}},\qquad
f_2=\frac{b_S-\mu_{b,T}qvec}{\sqrt{t_1v_{b,T}}}.              \tag{2}
\]
The finite supported-variance envelope makes every denominator in (2) positive.  The four exact orthogonality assumptions give \(e_1,e_2\in U_0^\perp\) and \(f_1,f_2\in V_0^\perp\).  For \(\beta=\gamma+\sigma x/\sqrt m\), define
\[
P_x=\frac{H-(\beta-\gamma)D}{\sigma\sqrt T}.
\]
Substitution of the definitions of \(H,D,\delta\), and the four vectors in (2) gives the exact identity
\[
P_x=(e_1,e_2)B_{NT,h}(x)(f_1,f_2)^{\top}.                    \tag{3}
\]
Indeed, the common scalar multiplying the heterogeneous part is
\[
\frac{\theta\sqrt{n_1t_1}}{\sigma\sqrt{mT}}
=h\sqrt{\frac Nm}\sqrt{p_Nq_T}=h\kappa_{NT},
\]
and the scalar multiplying the coefficient displacement is \(x\kappa_{NT}\).  Thus (3) also verifies the rectangular normalization in the claimed profile.

Complete orthonormal bases beginning with bases of \(U_0\) and \(V_0\).  Gaussian orthogonal invariance and (3) yield
\[
\frac{Y-\beta D}{\sigma\sqrt T}
=\begin{pmatrix}G+Z_{11}&Z_{12}\\Z_{21}&Z_{22}+P_x\end{pmatrix},              \tag{4}
\]
where \(s_r(G)\geq C_0\sqrt m\), every entry of \(Z=(Z_{jk})\) is independent \(\mathcal N(0,1/T)\), and the nonzero block of \(P_x\) has the two-by-two representation in (3).  The cited rectangular Gaussian outlier result, applied with zero perturbation, also gives \(\|Z\|_{\mathrm{op}}=O_p(1)\).  Hence, uniformly for \(|x|\leq M\), the lower blocks of every unit singular vector belonging to one of the first \(r\) singular values in (4) have norm \(O_p(m^{-1/2})\).  This follows directly from the two lower block equations for a singular pair: their left sides have singular value at least \(C_0\sqrt m-O_p(1)\), whereas all off-diagonal blocks have bounded operator norm.

For completeness, interpolate from \(P_0\) to \(P_x\).  At differentiability points, the derivative of the sum of the first \(r\) squared singular values is twice the Frobenius inner product of the perturbation with the lower-right block of the corresponding rank-\(r\) truncated singular-value expansion.  By the preceding lower-block bounds, that lower-right block is \(O_p(m^{-1/2})\).  The sum of squared singular values is locally Lipschitz, so integration across the finitely many nondifferentiability points gives
\[
\sup_{|x|\leq M}\left|
\sum_{j=1}^{r}s_j(G+Z+P_x)^2-\sum_{j=1}^{r}s_j(G+Z+P_0)^2
\right|=o_p(1).                                               \tag{5}
\]
Applying the same block equations to the symmetric dilation of (4), and eliminating the coordinates in the strong block, gives a Schur-complement error bounded by
\(C\|Z\|_{\mathrm{op}}^2/s_r(G)\).  Therefore
\[
\sup_{|x|\leq M}\left|s_{r+1}(G+Z+P_x)-s_1(Z_{22}+P_x)\right|=o_p(1).          \tag{6}
\]
Equations (5)--(6) are uniform because \(P_x\) ranges over a compact set and the lower bound in (1) is uniform.

We next record why the cited pointwise outlier theorem is sufficient here.  For any compact collection of deterministic two-by-two matrices, take a finite Frobenius \(\epsilon\)-net.  Gaussian invariance makes the law depend only on the singular values of the perturbation.  Weyl's inequality gives
\[
|s_1(Z_{22}+P)-s_1(Z_{22}+\widetilde P)|\leq\|P-\widetilde P\|_F.             \tag{7}
\]
The noise operator norm is tight, and \((\rho,s)\mapsto\psi_\rho(s)\) is continuous at the spectral edge because the two displayed branches agree when \(s=\rho^{1/4}\).  The finite net, (7), and then \(\epsilon\downarrow0\) upgrade the cited convergence to uniform convergence over the compact collection.  If \(c>1\), apply the cited result to \(c^{-1/2}(Z_{22}+P_x)^{\top}\), whose aspect ratio tends to \(1/c\); multiplying the resulting squared singular value by \(c\) gives exactly
\[
\psi_c(s)=
\begin{cases}
(1+\sqrt c)^2,&s\leq c^{1/4},\\
s^2+1+c+c/s^2,&s>c^{1/4}.
\end{cases}                                                     \tag{8}
\]
Replacing \((N,T)\) by \((N-r,T-r)\), and variance \(1/(T-r)\) by \(1/T\), changes (8) by \(o(1)\).  A subsequence contradiction, using compactness of the nuisance set, proves the same assertion uniformly when \(c_N\), rather than a fixed \(c\), varies in the maintained aspect envelope.  Consequently,
\[
\sup_{|x|\leq M}\left|s_1(Z_{22}+P_x)^2-\psi_{c_N}\{s_1(B_{NT,h}(x))\}\right|
\xrightarrow{p}0.                                               \tag{9}
\]

The Frobenius part has no omitted term.  Orthogonality of \(P_x\) to the strong block gives
\[
\left\|\frac{Y-\beta D}{\sigma\sqrt T}\right\|_F^2
-\left\|\frac{Y-\gamma D}{\sigma\sqrt T}\right\|_F^2
=\|B_{NT,h}(x)\|_F^2-\|B_{NT,h}(0)\|_F^2
+2\langle Z,P_x-P_0\rangle_F.                                  \tag{10}
\]
The last term is affine in \(x\), has mean zero, and on \(|x|\leq M\) has variance bounded by \(C_M/T\); hence its supremum is \(o_p(1)\).  The exact profile identity in \(\mathrm{def{:}full\mbox{-}profile}\), followed by (5), (6), (9), and (10), proves the asserted compact-profile convergence.

It remains to justify that a minimizer cannot escape the compact coordinate sets on which this convergence was established.  Write
\[
R=\kappa^2h^2(\mu_a^2+v_a)(\mu_b^2+v_b),\qquad
L_\infty=\kappa^2h^2v_av_b-(1+c).                               \tag{11}
\]
At \(x=0\), the matrix \(B_{\eta,h}(0)\) has rank one and squared singular value \(R\).  If \(R\leq\sqrt c\), then
\[
L_\infty-\Phi_{\eta,h}(0)
=2\sqrt c-\kappa^2h^2(\mu_a^2v_b+v_a\mu_b^2)\geq\sqrt c.       \tag{12}
\]
If \(R>\sqrt c\), then
\[
L_\infty-\Phi_{\eta,h}(0)=\kappa^2h^2v_av_b+c/R>0.             \tag{13}
\]
The right sides of (12)--(13) have a positive infimum on the maintained compact nuisance-signal set: in the second case use \(c\geq\underline c\) and the finite upper bound on \(R\).

To identify the tail, let \(e=e_1\), \(f=f_1\), and write the lower block as \(-t ef^{\top}+A\), where \(|t|=\kappa_{NT}|x|\) and \(\|A\|_{\mathrm{op}}=O_p(1)\).  Direct second-order expansion of the top eigenvalue of \((-t ef^{\top}+A)(-t ef^{\top}+A)^{\top}\) gives
\[
s_1(-t ef^{\top}+A)^2
=t^2-2t\,e^{\top}Af+\|A^{\top}e\|_2^2
+\|(I-ee^{\top})Af\|_2^2+O_p(|t|^{-1}).                        \tag{14}
\]
The remainder is uniform once \(|t|\) exceeds a fixed constant because \(\|A\|_{\mathrm{op}}=O_p(1)\).  For the Gaussian part of \(A\), the two quadratic terms in (14) converge to \(1\) and \(c\), respectively; their cross terms with the bounded deterministic spike converge to zero.  After cancellation with the Frobenius terms in (10), the deterministic remainder is
\[
\|(I-ee^{\top})P_0(I-ff^{\top})\|_F^2-(1+c)
=\kappa^2h^2v_av_b-(1+c)=L_\infty.                              \tag{15}
\]
The same expansion applied to the joint \((r+1)\)-dimensional diverging block covers sequences with \(|x|\) comparable to \(\sqrt m\); exact two-sided orthogonality makes the baseline and treatment blocks orthogonal before adding noise.  Thus every sequence \(|x_{NT}|\to\infty\) allowed by \(\gamma+\sigma x_{NT}/\sqrt m\in\mathcal B\) has profiled objective, relative to the common terms, converging to (15).  Equations (12)--(15) yield constants \(M_0<\infty\) and \(\epsilon_0>0\), uniform on the compact parameter set, such that with probability tending to one every global minimizer lies in \([-M_0,M_0]\).

On this last compact interval, the proved uniform criterion convergence applies.  By the definition of \(\mathcal G_{\mathrm{stab}}\), every limiting criterion has a unique minimizer and a positive separation outside each neighborhood of it.  Compactness upgrades this to a common separation modulus.  Since \(\eta_{NT}\to\eta\) and \(\Phi_{NT,h}\to\Phi_{\eta,h}\) uniformly on compacts, the deterministic sets \(\mathcal S_{NT}(h)\) lie in that neighborhood as well.  The standard contradiction proof of the argmin lemma now uses only the displayed separation: if \(\operatorname{dist}\{\widehat x_F,\mathcal S_{NT}(h)\}\geq\epsilon\), the deterministic criterion gap is bounded below while the stochastic sup-norm error tends to zero.  This is impossible with probability bounded away from zero.  It proves both the distance assertion and uniform \(O_p(1)\) localization.  A genuine limiting tie lacks the required separation, which is exactly why it is excluded from the conclusion.

Let \(x_A=h\mu_a\mu_b=x_{\operatorname{ATT}}\).  Substituting \(x_A\) into the two-by-two profile gives
\[
\|B_{\eta,h}(x_A)\|_F^2
=\kappa^2h^2(\mu_a^2v_b+v_a\mu_b^2+v_av_b)<\sqrt c.             \tag{16}
\]
Therefore \(s_1(B_{\eta,h}(x_A))<c^{1/4}\).  On the entire subcritical part of the scalar line the definition of \(\psi_c\) yields
\[
\Phi_{\eta,h}(x)=\|B_{\eta,h}(x)\|_F^2-(1+\sqrt c)^2,          \tag{17}
\]
and the only term in the squared norm depending on \(x\) is \(\kappa^2(h\mu_a\mu_b-x)^2\).  Thus (17) is uniquely minimized at \(x_A\) among subcritical points.

For every supercritical \(x\), write \(s_j=s_j(B_{\eta,h}(x))\).  Since \(s_1^2>\sqrt c\),
\[
\Phi_{\eta,h}(x)
=s_2^2-(1+c)-\frac c{s_1^2}>-(1+c)-\sqrt c.                    \tag{18}
\]
On the other hand, (16)--(17) imply
\[
\Phi_{\eta,h}(x_A)<\sqrt c-(1+\sqrt c)^2
=-(1+c)-\sqrt c.                                               \tag{19}
\]
Equations (18)--(19) rule out every supercritical competitor, proving \(\mathcal S(\eta,h)=\{x_A\}\).

On a compact subset satisfying the strict inequality in (16), compactness supplies a common positive margin.  Since \(\eta_{NT}\to\eta\), the corresponding finite-array inequality holds eventually, and the same calculation gives
\(\mathcal S_{NT}(h)=\{h\mu_{a,N}\mu_{b,T}\}\).  The distance conclusion of \(\mathrm{thm{:}uniform\mbox{-}profile}\) then gives
\[
\frac{\sqrt m(\widehat\beta_F-\operatorname{ATT}_{NT})}{\sigma}
=\widehat x_F-h\mu_{a,N}\mu_{b,T}\xrightarrow{p}0,
\]
uniformly on that compact subset.  Every division used above is justified by \(\kappa>0\), \(c>0\), and the positive supported variances in \(\mathcal E_{\mathrm{loc}}\).

The exact finite-array identity is
\[
\frac{\sqrt m(\widehat\beta_F-\operatorname{ATT}_{NT})}{\sigma}
=\widehat x_F-h\mu_{a,N}\mu_{b,T}.                             \tag{20}
\]
By \(\mathrm{thm{:}uniform\mbox{-}profile}\), the first term on the right is at vanishing distance from \(\mathcal S_{NT}(h)\).  The functions \(\Phi_{NT,h}\) converge uniformly on compact scalar sets to \(\Phi_{\eta,h}\), because \(\eta_{NT}\to\eta\), the singular-value map is Lipschitz, and \(\psi_c\) is jointly continuous, including at \(s=c^{1/4}\).  The tail separation (12)--(15) localizes both deterministic argmin sets.  On a compact subset of \(\mathcal G_{\mathrm{loc}}\), uniqueness and the defining separation of \(\mathcal G_{\mathrm{stab}}\) then imply
\[
\sup \operatorname{dist}\{\mathcal S_{NT}(h),x_\star(\eta,h)\}\longrightarrow0.  \tag{21}
\]
This is the same elementary separated-argmin contradiction used at the end of the preceding proof.  Finally, the moment assumptions give
\(\mu_{a,N}\mu_{b,T}\to\mu_a\mu_b\).  Substitution of (21) into (20) proves the displayed absorption law uniformly on each such compact set.

The deleted existential clause cannot be deduced from the frozen assumptions.  Indeed, the admissible constants may satisfy
\[
\overline h^{,2}\max\{\overline c,1\}(1-\underline\pi)^2
\bigl(2\overline\mu^{,2}\overline v+\overline v^{,2}\bigr)
<\sqrt{\underline c}.                                         \tag{22}
\]
Condition (22) is compatible with every frozen assumption by choosing the otherwise unrestricted positive constant \(K\) sufficiently small.  It implies the strict subcritical inequality (16) for every \((\eta,h)\in\mathcal E_{\mathrm{loc}}\times[-\overline h,\overline h]\).  The proved subcritical theorem then gives \(x_\star=h\mu_a\mu_b\) everywhere in \(\mathcal G_{\mathrm{loc}}\), so no nonempty absorbed subset can exist.  This is a generic admissible-class certificate, not merely a single numerical counterexample.

Let \(e_1,f_1\) be the treatment-support basis vectors in (2).  The strong-factor block calculation in (4)--(6), now evaluated at \(\widehat x_F\), shows that the first \(r\) selected left and right singular spaces converge to \(U_0\) and \(V_0\), while the additional selected singular pair is the leading pair of
\(Z_{22}+P_{\widehat x_F}\).  The absorption law and the separated argmin property give \(\widehat x_F\to x_\star\).  At a strictly subcritical point, the cited singular-vector theorem gives
\[
|\langle\widehat u,e_1\rangle|^2\xrightarrow{p}0,\qquad
|\langle\widehat v,f_1\rangle|^2\xrightarrow{p}0.              \tag{23}
\]
At a simple strictly supercritical point, take the singular-value decomposition of the two-by-two population spike.  The cited theorem, followed for \(c>1\) by the same transpose-and-rescale argument used in (8), gives
\[
|\langle\widehat u,e_1\rangle|^2
 \xrightarrow{p}\ell_c(s_\star)u_{\star,1}^2,\qquad
|\langle\widehat v,f_1\rangle|^2
 \xrightarrow{p}r_c(s_\star)v_{\star,1}^2.                    \tag{24}
\]
The projections on all distinct population spike directions vanish, which justifies the factors \(u_{\star,1}^2\) and \(v_{\star,1}^2\) in (24).  Strict separation from the edge and simplicity make (23)--(24) uniform on compact subsets of the stated regular set.

Since \(D=\sqrt{n_1t_1}\,e_1f_1^{\top}\), while \(e_1\perp U_0\) and \(f_1\perp V_0\),
\[
\frac{\|\widetilde D\|_F}{\sqrt{NT}}
=\sqrt{p_Nq_T}\,\|(I-P_{\widehat U})e_1\|_2
                   \|(I-P_{\widehat V})f_1\|_2.               \tag{25}
\]
Substitution of (23) or (24) into (25) proves the asserted formula for \(a_D\).  In the supercritical case, \(0<\ell_c(s)<1\) and \(0<r_c(s)<1\) for every finite \(s>c^{1/4}\); hence the two factors in braces are strictly positive even if a first singular-vector coordinate has absolute value one.  Compactness gives a common positive lower bound.

We next prove variance consistency rather than assuming it.  From the absorption law, \(\widehat\beta_F-\gamma=O_p(m^{-1/2})\).  Thus the nonbaseline signal in \(Y-\widehat\beta_FD\) has squared Frobenius norm \(O_p(T)\), because \(N/T\) is bounded above and below.  The matrix \(Y-\widehat\beta_FD\) differs from \(E\) by a matrix of rank at most \(r+2\).  Singular-value interlacing for a rank-\((r+2)\) perturbation bounds its residual sum of squares after deletion of \(r+1\) singular values between noise residual sums obtained by deleting fixed numbers of singular values, up to the preceding \(O_p(T)\) signal term and its Cauchy--Schwarz cross term.  The Gaussian law of large numbers gives
\[
\frac{\|E\|_F^2}{NT}\xrightarrow{p}\sigma^2,\qquad
\frac1{NT}\sum_{j=1}^{2r+3}s_j(E)^2=O_p(N^{-1})=o_p(1).         \tag{26}
\]
The signal contribution divided by \(NT\) is \(O_p(N^{-1})\), and its cross term divided by \(NT\) is \(O_p(N^{-1/2})\).  Hence
\[
\frac{\|Y-\widehat\beta_FD-\widehat L_F\|_F^2}{NT}
\xrightarrow{p}\sigma^2.                                     \tag{27}
\]
Because \(r\) is fixed and \(N/T\) stays in a compact subset of \((0,\infty)\), \(\nu_F/(NT)\to1\), so (27) proves \(\widehat\sigma_F\xrightarrow{p}\sigma\).

Finally set \(b(\eta,h)=x_\star(\eta,h)-h\mu_a\mu_b\).  On a compact subset of the stated absorbed set, \(|b|\) is bounded away from zero.  The absorption law gives
\[
\frac{\sqrt m(\widehat\beta_F-\operatorname{ATT}_{NT})}{\sigma}
\xrightarrow{p}b(\eta,h),                                    \tag{28}
\]
whereas (25), (27), and \(NT\asymp m^2\) give
\[
\frac{\sqrt m}{\sigma}
\frac{z_{1-\alpha/2}\widehat\sigma_F}{\|\widetilde D\|_F}
=O_p(m^{-1/2})\longrightarrow0.                               \tag{29}
\]
The event that the interval contains the target requires the absolute value of the left side of (28) to be no larger than (29).  Equations (28)--(29) therefore make its probability tend to zero, uniformly on compact subsets.  The small-radius certificate (22) also shows why nonemptiness of this regular absorbed set cannot follow from the frozen assumptions alone.

At \(\theta=0\), the noise-scale bound implies \(h=0\), while the definition of the causal target gives \(\operatorname{ATT}_{NT}=\gamma\).  Moreover,
\[
B_{\eta,0}(x)=-\kappa x e_{11},\qquad
s_1\{B_{\eta,0}(x)\}=\kappa|x|.                               \tag{30}
\]
If \(\kappa|x|\leq c^{1/4}\), then
\[
\Phi_{\eta,0}(x)=\kappa^2x^2-(1+\sqrt c)^2,
\]
which is uniquely minimized at zero.  If \(\kappa|x|>c^{1/4}\), then
\[
\Phi_{\eta,0}(x)=-(1+c)-\frac{c}{\kappa^2x^2}
>-(1+c)-\sqrt c
>-(1+c)-2\sqrt c=\Phi_{\eta,0}(0).                             \tag{31}
\]
Thus \(\mathcal S(\eta,0)=\{0\}\), with strict global separation.  Applying \(\mathrm{thm{:}uniform\mbox{-}profile}\) yields \(\widehat x_F\to_p0\), equivalently \(\sqrt m(\widehat\beta_F-\gamma)/\sigma\to_p0\).  Together with \(\operatorname{ATT}_{NT}=\gamma\), this proves every assertion.

Suppose \(0<c\leq1\), \(N/T\to c\), and \(Z_{NT}=E/(\sigma\sqrt T)\).  Let a deterministic fixed-rank perturbation have a simple largest singular value \(s>c^{1/4}\), with corresponding unit left and right singular vectors \(u\) and \(v\).  If \(\widehat u\) and \(\widehat v\) are the singular vectors associated with the resulting largest outlier, then
\[
|\langle\widehat u,u\rangle|^2\longrightarrow
\frac{s^4-c}{s^2(s^2+c)},\qquad
|\langle\widehat v,v\rangle|^2\longrightarrow
\frac{s^4-c}{s^2(s^2+1)}
\]
almost surely, while their projections on population singular-vector spaces belonging to distinct spikes converge to zero.  If every perturbation singular value is strictly below \(c^{1/4}\), the projections of an edge singular vector on the fixed perturbation spaces converge to zero.

theorem.statement:
Suppose \(\eta\in\mathcal E_{\mathrm{loc}}\) and \(h\in\mathbb R\).  Then \((\eta,h)\in\mathcal G_{\mathrm{stab}}\): the set \(\mathcal S(\eta,h)\) is always a separated singleton.  Its member \(x_\star(\eta,h)\) is given by the following explicit scalar map.  If \(h=0\), then \(x_\star(\eta,0)=0\).  If \(h\neq0\), define
\[
 s=\operatorname{sgn}(h\mu_a\mu_b),\quad
 z_0=\kappa|h\mu_a\mu_b|,\quad
 b_0=\kappa|h\mu_a|\sqrt{v_b},\quad
 c_0=\kappa|h\mu_b|\sqrt{v_a},\quad
 d_0=\kappa|h|\sqrt{v_av_b},
\]
and, for \(0\leq z\leq z_0\), put
\[
 w=z_0-z,\qquad Q(z)=z^2+b_0^2+c_0^2+d_0^2,
\]
\[
 \tau(z)=\frac{Q(z)+\sqrt{Q(z)^2-4d_0^2w^2}}2,qquad
 \mathcal R(z)=\frac{d_0^2w\tau(z)\{\tau(z)+zw\}}
 {z\tau(z)+d_0^2w}.
\]
Let \(z_\star=0\) when \(\tau(0)^2\leq c\); when \(\tau(0)^2>c\), let \(z_\star\) be the unique root of \(\mathcal R(z)=c\) in \((0,z_0)\).  Then
\[
 \mathcal S(\eta,h)=\{x_\star(\eta,h)\},\qquad
 x_\star(\eta,h)=\frac{s}{\kappa}(z_0-z_\star).
\]
The map \((\eta,h)\mapsto x_\star(\eta,h)\) is continuous.  For every compact \(\mathcal K\subset\mathcal E_{\mathrm{loc}}\times\mathbb R\) and every \(\varepsilon>0\),
\[
 \inf_{(\eta,h)\in\mathcal K}\ \inf_{|x-x_\star(\eta,h)|\geq\varepsilon}
 \left\{\Phi_{\eta,h}(x)-\Phi_{\eta,h}\bigl(x_\star(\eta,h)\bigr)\right\}>0. \tag{8}
\]
Consequently, let \((\eta_n,h_n)\in\mathcal K\), let \(C_n:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R\) be random criteria, and let \(\widehat x_n\) be any measurable global minimizer.  If \(\widehat x_n\) is uniformly tight and, for every finite \(M\),
\[
 \sup_{|x|\leq M}\left|
 \{C_n(x)-C_n(x_\star(\eta_n,h_n))\}
 -\{\Phi_{\eta_n,h_n}(x)-\Phi_{\eta_n,h_n}(x_\star(\eta_n,h_n))\}
 \right|\xrightarrow{p}0,
\]
then \(\widehat x_n-x_\star(\eta_n,h_n)\xrightarrow{p}0\).  Thus no coefficient-indexed next-order noise process is needed to break a first-order tie.

The critical selection is one-sided but remains unique.  At a point with \(h\neq0\) and \(\tau(0)^2=c\), consider any admissible path indexed by \(\epsilon\downarrow0\) for which
\[
 \Delta_\epsilon=\tau_\epsilon(0)^2-c_\epsilon
 =\epsilon\dot\Delta+o(\epsilon).
\]
Writing \(\mathcal R_0'(0)<0\) for the derivative at the limiting point, one has
\[
 z_{\star,\epsilon}
 =\epsilon\frac{(\dot\Delta)_+}{-\mathcal R_0'(0)}+o(\epsilon),
\qquad
 x_{\star,\epsilon}-h_\epsilon\mu_{a,\epsilon}\mu_{b,\epsilon}
 =-\frac{s}{\kappa}\epsilon
 \frac{(\dot\Delta)_+}{-\mathcal R_0'(0)}+o(\epsilon).
\]
In particular, opposite admissible \(m^{-1/4}\) drifts can change this local directional derivative, but both selections converge to the same critical minimizer; they cannot produce different separated limiting selections with identical limiting nuisance coordinates.
theorem.proof_tex:
The condition \(\eta\in\mathcal E_{\mathrm{loc}}\) gives \(c,p,q,v_a,v_b>0\), \(\mu_a\mu_b\neq0\), and hence \(\kappa>0\).  First suppose \(h\neq0\).  Let
\[
 U=\operatorname{diag}\{\operatorname{sgn}(\mu_a),1\},\qquad
 V=\operatorname{diag}\{\operatorname{sgn}(h\mu_b),\operatorname{sgn}(h)\}.
\]
Both matrices are orthogonal.  Substitution in the definition of \(B_{\eta,h}(x)\) gives
\[
 UB_{\eta,h}(x)V
 =\begin{pmatrix}z&b_0\\c_0&d_0\end{pmatrix},
 \qquad z=z_0-s\kappa x,
\]
with \(s,z_0,b_0,c_0,d_0\) exactly as stated.  In particular, all three fixed entries are strictly positive and
\[
 \frac{b_0c_0}{d_0}=z_0.
\]
Orthogonal multiplication preserves both the Frobenius norm and singular values.  Since \(x\mapsto z_0-s\kappa x\) is a bijection of \(\mathbb R\), the scalar-profile lemma with \(\rho=c\) applies verbatim.  It proves that the displayed \(z_\star\) is the unique separated minimizer and that its inverse image is
\[
 x_\star=\frac{s}{\kappa}(z_0-z_\star).
\]
This also shows directly that \(x_\star=h\mu_a\mu_b\) on the subcritical side and that it lies strictly between zero and \(h\mu_a\mu_b\) on the supercritical side.

If \(h=0\), then \(B_{\eta,0}(x)=-\kappa x e_{11}\).  For \(\kappa^2x^2\leq\sqrt c\), direct substitution gives
\[
 \Phi_{\eta,0}(x)=\kappa^2x^2-(1+\sqrt c)^2,
\]
which is uniquely minimized at zero.  For \(\kappa^2x^2>\sqrt c\), it gives
\[
 \Phi_{\eta,0}(x)=-(1+c)-\frac{c}{\kappa^2x^2}
 >-(1+\sqrt c)^2=\Phi_{\eta,0}(0).
\]
Thus zero is again the unique separated minimizer.

We next establish continuity and uniform separation.  The explicit construction always gives
\[
 |x_\star(\eta,h)|\leq |h\mu_a\mu_b|. \tag{9}
\]
Consider a convergent sequence of admissible parameter points.  Bound (9) makes the corresponding minimizers bounded.  Every subsequential limit minimizes the limiting continuous profile, because the displayed two-by-two formulas converge uniformly on bounded \(x\)-sets.  The limiting minimizer is unique by the preceding argument, so every subsequence has the same limit.  This proves continuity of \(x_\star\), including at \(h=0\) and at \(\tau(0)^2=c\).

For completeness, the tail separation used here is uniform on compact parameter sets.  In the rotated coordinate,
\[
 \lim_{|z|\to\infty}\Phi_{\eta,h}(x(z))=d_0^2-(1+c).
\]
At the rank-one point \(z_0\), with \(S=z_0^2+b_0^2+c_0^2+d_0^2\), the tail value exceeds the profile value by
\[
 \begin{cases}
 d_0^2+2\sqrt c-S,&S\leq\sqrt c,\\
 d_0^2+c/S,&S>\sqrt c.
 \end{cases}
\]
The first expression is at least \(d_0^2+\sqrt c\), and the second is positive.  These gaps, the profiles, and their unique minimizers vary continuously; the convergence to the tail is uniform when the parameters range over a compact subset of \(\mathcal E_{\mathrm{loc}}\times\mathbb R\).  Therefore a failure of (8) would yield, by compactness and passage to a subsequence, either a second finite minimizer of a limiting profile or a tail value equal to its minimum.  Both conclusions contradict what was just proved.  This establishes (8).  The standard deterministic argmin comparison is immediate from (8): outside any fixed neighborhood of \(x_\star\), the limiting criterion has a uniform positive gap, and a uniformly vanishing criterion error cannot reverse that gap.  Uniform localization handles the complement of the compact \(x\)-set.  Hence no next-order stochastic selector is required.

Finally consider a critical admissible path.  The scalar lemma proves \(\mathcal R_0'(0)<0\).  If \(\Delta_\epsilon\leq0\), the exact selection rule gives \(z_{\star,\epsilon}=0\).  If \(\Delta_\epsilon>0\), the defining equation is
\[
 \mathcal R_\epsilon(z_{\star,\epsilon})-c_\epsilon=0.
\]
Continuity first gives \(z_{\star,\epsilon}\to0\).  A first-order expansion at zero then yields
\[
 0=\Delta_\epsilon+\mathcal R_0'(0)z_{\star,\epsilon}
 +o(\epsilon+z_{\star,\epsilon}),
\]
and the strict nonzero derivative implies
\[
 z_{\star,\epsilon}=\epsilon(\dot\Delta)_+/\{-\mathcal R_0'(0)\}+o(\epsilon).
\]
Because \(s\) is locally constant and \(s z_{0,\epsilon}/\kappa_\epsilon=h_\epsilon\mu_{a,\epsilon}\mu_{b,\epsilon}\), inversion of the rotated coordinate gives the claimed expansion for \(x_{\star,\epsilon}\).  Taking \(\epsilon=m^{-1/4}\) on opposite paths changes only the displayed directional term, which vanishes without rescaling.  Thus the proposed separated-tie obstruction does not occur anywhere in the admissible geometry.

added_lemmas.statement:
Let \(\rho,b_0,c_0,d_0>0\), let \(z_0=b_0c_0/d_0\), and set
\[
 M(z)=\begin{pmatrix}z&b_0\\ c_0&d_0\end{pmatrix},\qquad
 \varphi_\rho(z)=\|M(z)\|_F^2-\Psi_\rho\{s_1(M(z))\},
\]
where
\[
 \Psi_\rho(s)=(1+\sqrt\rho)^2\mathbf 1\{s\leq \rho^{1/4}\}
 +\left(s^2+1+\rho+\frac{\rho}{s^2}\right)\mathbf 1\{s>\rho^{1/4}\}.
\]
For \(0\leq z\leq z_0\), write \(w=z_0-z\),
\[
 Q(z)=z^2+b_0^2+c_0^2+d_0^2,\qquad
 \tau(z)=\frac{Q(z)+\sqrt{Q(z)^2-4d_0^2w^2}}{2},
\]
and
\[
 \mathcal R(z)=\frac{d_0^2w\tau(z)\{\tau(z)+zw\}}
 {z\tau(z)+d_0^2w}.
\]
Then \(\varphi_\rho\) has exactly one global minimizer.  It is \(z_\star=0\) if \(\tau(0)^2\leq\rho\).  If \(\tau(0)^2>\rho\), it is the unique \(z_\star\in(0,z_0)\) satisfying \(\mathcal R(z_\star)=\rho\).  In either case, for every \(\varepsilon>0\),
\[
 \inf_{|z-z_\star|\geq\varepsilon}
 \{\varphi_\rho(z)-\varphi_\rho(z_\star)\}>0.
\]
added_lemmas.proof_tex:
Let \(\tau(z)=s_1\{M(z)\}^2\) and \(u(z)=s_2\{M(z)\}^2\).  The trace and determinant identities for the two eigenvalues of \(M(z)M(z)^{\top}\) give
\[
 \tau+u=Q(z),\qquad \tau u=d_0^2(z-z_0)^2.
\]
This proves the displayed formula for \(\tau\), and, whenever \(\tau>0\), gives \(u=d_0^2(z-z_0)^2/\tau\).  Define
\[
 G_\rho(t)=
 \begin{cases}
 0,&t\leq\sqrt\rho,\\
 t+\rho/t-2\sqrt\rho,&t>\sqrt\rho.
 \end{cases}
\]
Direct substitution in the definition of \(\Psi_\rho\) yields
\[
 \varphi_\rho(z)=z^2+b_0^2+c_0^2+d_0^2-(1+\sqrt\rho)^2-G_\rho\{\tau(z)\}. \tag{1}
\]
The function \(G_\rho\) is nondecreasing, is continuously differentiable, and has derivative zero below the edge and \(1-\rho/t^2\) above the edge.

We first localize the minimum.  If \(q>0\), then \(Q(-q)=Q(q)\), whereas
\[
 |\det M(-q)|=d_0(q+z_0)\geq d_0|q-z_0|=|\det M(q)|.
\]
For two nonnegative roots with fixed sum \(Q(q)\), the larger root is nonincreasing in their product.  Hence \(\tau(-q)\leq\tau(q)\), and (1) implies \(\varphi_\rho(-q)\geq\varphi_\rho(q)\).

For \(z>z_0\), the top squared singular value is simple because the off-diagonal entry \(zc_0+b_0d_0\) of \(M(z)M(z)^{\top}\) is positive.  Put \(v=z-z_0>0\).  Differentiating
\[
 \tau^2-Q(z)\tau+d_0^2v^2=0
\]
gives
\[
 \tau'(z)=\frac{2\{z\tau-d_0^2v\}}{\tau-u}.
\]
Moreover, \(\tau\geq z^2+c_0^2>zv\), so
\[
 2z-\tau'(z)=\frac{2d_0^2v\{1-zv/\tau\}}{\tau-u}>0. \tag{2}
\]
Below the spectral edge, (1) has derivative \(2z>0\).  Above the edge its derivative is
\[
 2z-\left(1-\frac{\rho}{\tau^2}\right)\tau'(z),
\]
which is positive by (2), whether \(\tau'\) is nonnegative or negative.  Thus \(\varphi_\rho\) is strictly increasing on \((z_0,\infty)\).  Together with the preceding reflection comparison, every global minimizer lies in \([0,z_0]\).

It remains to analyze this interval.  Put \(w=z_0-z\).  Here the same characteristic equation gives
\[
 \tau'(z)=\frac{2\{z\tau+d_0^2w\}}{\tau-u}>0. \tag{3}
\]
The strict inequality follows because every term in the numerator is nonnegative and \(d_0^2w>0\) away from \(z_0\); continuity covers the endpoint.  In the supercritical region, (1) and (3) imply
\[
 \varphi_\rho'(z)
 =\frac{\tau'(z)}{\tau(z)^2}\{\rho-\mathcal R(z)\}, \tag{4}
\]
because
\[
 \tau^2\left(1-\frac{2z}{\tau'}\right)
 =\frac{d_0^2w\tau(\tau+zw)}{z\tau+d_0^2w}
 =\mathcal R(z). \tag{5}
\]
Also, \(\mathcal R(0)=\tau(0)^2\) and \(\lim_{z\uparrow z_0}\mathcal R(z)=0\).

We now prove the load-bearing monotonicity rather than assuming it.  For \(0\leq z<z_0\), define
\[
 \alpha=\frac{d_0}{w},\qquad \xi=\frac{z}{w},\qquad
 y=\frac{\tau}{d_0w},\qquad e=\frac{(b_0-c_0)^2}{w^2}.
\]
The two singular values cannot be equal, since \(zc_0+b_0d_0>0\); hence \(y>1\).  The characteristic equation and \(b_0c_0=d_0(z+w)\) imply
\[
 \alpha\left(y+\frac1y\right)
 =\xi^2+\alpha^2+2\alpha(1+\xi)+e. \tag{6}
\]
Differentiate the right side of (5), use (3), and then use (6).  Collecting terms gives the exact factorization
\[
 \mathcal R'(z)
 =-\frac{d_0^5\tau w^6}
 {(\tau^2-d_0^2w^2)(d_0^2w+\tau z)^2}
 \left[\alpha(1+\xi)(y-1)^3(y+3)+4ey\right]<0. \tag{7}
\]
Every denominator in (7) is positive, and the bracket is strictly positive because \(\alpha>0\), \(1+\xi>0\), and \(y>1\).  Thus \(\mathcal R\) decreases strictly from \(\tau(0)^2\) to zero.

If \(\tau(0)^2\leq\rho\), then (3) shows that any subcritical portion has derivative \(2z>0\), while on any supercritical portion (4) and (7) give \(\varphi_\rho'(z)>0\) for \(z>0\).  Hence zero is the unique minimizer.  If \(\tau(0)^2>\rho\), then zero is supercritical and (4) is negative at zero.  Equations (4) and (7) show that the derivative changes sign exactly once, at the unique solution of \(\mathcal R(z)=\rho\).  At that solution \(\rho=\mathcal R(z)<\tau(z)^2\), so it indeed lies in the supercritical region.  The derivative is negative before this root and positive after it, proving global uniqueness.

Finally,
\[
 \lim_{|z|\to\infty}\varphi_\rho(z)=d_0^2-(1+\rho).
\]
At the rank-one point \(z_0\), put \(S=z_0^2+b_0^2+c_0^2+d_0^2\).  If \(S\leq\sqrt\rho\), the difference between this tail limit and \(\varphi_\rho(z_0)\) is \(d_0^2+2\sqrt\rho-S\geq d_0^2+\sqrt\rho>0\).  If \(S>\sqrt\rho\), that difference is \(d_0^2+\rho/S>0\).  The unique minimum is no larger than \(\varphi_\rho(z_0)\), so it is strictly below the tail limit.  Continuity, uniqueness on bounded sets, and this strict tail gap prove the asserted separation.

proofs.proof_tex:
Fix \(\eta\in\mathcal E_{\mathrm{loc}}\), and abbreviate
\[
 M=\mu_a\mu_b,\qquad U=\mu_a^2+v_a,\qquad V=\mu_b^2+v_b,\qquad R=v_av_b,\qquad L=UV.
\]
The definition of \(\mathcal E_{\mathrm{loc}}\) gives \(v_a>0\), \(v_b>0\), \(c>0\), \(p>0\), and \(q>0\).  Hence \(R>0\), \(L>0\), and \(\kappa=\sqrt{\max\{c,1\}pq}>0\).

For \(h\ne0\), put \(y=x/h\) and
\[
 C(y)=A_\eta-ye_{11}
 =\begin{pmatrix}
 M-y&\mu_a\sqrt{v_b}\\
 \sqrt{v_a}\mu_b&\sqrt{R}
 \end{pmatrix}.
\]
Let \(\tau(y)\) and \(\upsilon(y)\) be, respectively, the larger and smaller squared singular values of \(C(y)\).  Direct calculation gives
\[
 \|C(y)\|_F^2=L-2My+y^2,
 \qquad
 \det C(y)=-y\sqrt R.
\]
Consequently, using the trace and determinant identities for the two eigenvalues of \(C(y)C(y)^{\top}\),
\[
 \tau(y)+\upsilon(y)=L-2My+y^2,
 \qquad
 \tau(y)\upsilon(y)=Ry^2.                                      \tag{1}
\]
Moreover, the lower-right entry of \(C(y)\) is \(\sqrt R\), so
\[
 \tau(y)=s_1\{C(y)\}^2\ge R                                      \tag{2}
\]
for every \(y\in\mathbb R\).  At \(y=0\), equation \((1)\) yields
\[
 \tau(0)=L,\qquad \upsilon(0)=0.                                  \tag{3}
\]
Since \(R>0\), equations \((1)\)--\((2)\) also show that \(\upsilon(y)=0\) if and only if \(y=0\).

We next establish the global localization needed to justify using the local expansion.  The bounds
\[
 (M-y)^2\le \tau(y)\le \|C(y)\|_F^2=L-2My+y^2
\]
imply \(\tau(y)/y^2\to1\) as \(|y|\to\infty\).  By \((1)\), therefore,
\[
 \upsilon(y)=\frac{Ry^2}{\tau(y)}\longrightarrow R
 \quad\text{as }|y|\to\infty.                                    \tag{4}
\]
Thus \(\upsilon\) is continuous, has the unique zero \(0\), and is separated from zero off every neighborhood of zero: for each \(d>0\),
\[
 a_d:=\inf_{|y|\ge d}\upsilon(y)>0.                                \tag{5}
\]
Indeed, \((4)\) controls the tails, while continuity and the unique-zero property control the remaining compact set.

By the local-spike-profile definition,
\[
 B_{\eta,h}(hy)=\kappa h C(y).
\]
It follows from \((2)\) that
\[
 s_1\{B_{\eta,h}(hy)\}=\kappa|h|\sqrt{\tau(y)}
 \ge \kappa|h|\sqrt R.
\]
Hence, whenever \(\kappa|h|\sqrt R>c^{1/4}\), every \(y\) lies on the supercritical branch in the definition of \(\psi_c\).  On that branch,
\[
 \begin{aligned}
 \Phi_{\eta,h}(hy)
 &=\kappa^2h^2\{\tau(y)+\upsilon(y)\}
   -\left\{\kappa^2h^2\tau(y)+1+c+
   \frac{c}{\kappa^2h^2\tau(y)}\right\}\\
 &=\kappa^2h^2\left\{\upsilon(y)-
   \frac{\varepsilon_h}{\tau(y)}\right\}-(1+c),
 \qquad
 \varepsilon_h:=\frac{c}{\kappa^4h^4}.                            \tag{6}
 \end{aligned}
\]
Thus minimizing \(\Phi_{\eta,h}\) over \(x\in\mathbb R\) is equivalent to minimizing
\[
 g_\varepsilon(y):=\upsilon(y)-\frac{\varepsilon}{\tau(y)}         \tag{7}
\]
over \(y\in\mathbb R\), with \(\varepsilon=\varepsilon_h\).

We now prove that this minimizer is unique and global for all sufficiently small \(\varepsilon>0\).  At \(y=0\), equations \((3)\) and \((7)\) give
\[
 g_\varepsilon(0)=-\frac{\varepsilon}{L}<0.                        \tag{8}
\]
On the other hand, \((2)\), \((5)\), and \((7)\) give, for \(|y|\ge d\),
\[
 g_\varepsilon(y)\ge a_d-\frac{\varepsilon}{R}.                   \tag{9}
\]
Choose \(d>0\) small enough that the two roots in \((1)\) remain distinct on \([-d,d]\).  There, they are twice continuously differentiable, as is seen directly from the quadratic formula applied to \((1)\).  Differentiating \((1)\) at zero and using \((3)\) gives
\[
 \upsilon'(0)=0,\qquad \tau'(0)=-2M,
 \qquad \upsilon''(0)=\frac{2R}{L}>0.                              \tag{10}
\]
After decreasing \(d\) if necessary, \(\upsilon''\) is bounded below by a positive constant on \([-d,d]\).  Because \(\tau\ge R\) and \(\tau\) is twice continuously differentiable there, the second derivative of \(-\varepsilon/\tau\) is uniformly of order \(\varepsilon\).  Therefore \(g_\varepsilon\) is strictly convex on \([-d,d]\) for all sufficiently small \(\varepsilon\).  Equations \((8)\)--\((9)\), with \(\varepsilon<a_dR/2\), place every global minimizer in \((-d,d)\).  Such a minimizer exists by continuity on \([-d,d]\), and strict convexity makes it unique; denote it by \(y_\varepsilon\).

This uniqueness also supplies the separation required in \(\mathcal G_{\mathrm{stab}}\).  Indeed, \((4)\) and \((7)\) give \(g_\varepsilon(y)\to R>g_\varepsilon(y_\varepsilon)\) as \(|y|\to\infty\).  On every compact set excluding a fixed neighborhood of \(y_\varepsilon\), continuity and uniqueness give a strictly positive objective gap.  The change of variables \(x=hy\) and the positive rescaling in \((6)\) preserve this property.  Consequently, for all sufficiently large \(|h|\),
\[
 (\eta,h)\in\mathcal G_{\mathrm{stab}},
 \qquad x_\star(\eta,h)=h y_{\varepsilon_h}.                       \tag{11}
\]
This proves, in particular, the global localization that is needed rather than merely assuming a local stationary branch.

It remains to compute the branch.  Since \(y_{\varepsilon}\in(-d,d)\), its first-order condition is
\[
 0=g_\varepsilon'(y_\varepsilon)
 =\upsilon'(y_\varepsilon)
  +\varepsilon\frac{\tau'(y_\varepsilon)}{\tau(y_\varepsilon)^2}. \tag{12}
\]
The positive lower bound on \(\upsilon''\), together with \(\upsilon'(0)=0\), and the boundedness of \(\tau'/\tau^2\) near zero imply from \((12)\) that \(y_\varepsilon=O(\varepsilon)\).  Expanding \((12)\) with \((10)\) and \((3)\) therefore yields
\[
 0=\frac{2R}{L}y_\varepsilon
   -\frac{2M}{L^2}\varepsilon+o(\varepsilon),
\]
and hence
\[
 y_\varepsilon=\frac{M}{RL}\varepsilon+o(\varepsilon).            \tag{13}
\]
Substituting \(\varepsilon_h=c/(\kappa^4h^4)\), \(M=\mu_a\mu_b\), \(R=v_av_b\), and \(L=(\mu_a^2+v_a)(\mu_b^2+v_b)\) into \((11)\)--\((13)\) gives
\[
 x_\star(\eta,h)
 =\frac{c\mu_a\mu_b}
 {\kappa^4v_av_b(\mu_a^2+v_a)(\mu_b^2+v_b)}h^{-3}
 +o(h^{-3})
\]
as \(|h|\to\infty\), for either sign of \(h\).  In particular, \(x_\star(\eta,h)\to0\).  The argument varied only the deterministic scalar \(h\) in the limiting profile; it did not take a stochastic triangular-array limit.  It therefore establishes precisely the stated deterministic endpoint and makes no additional assertion for the bounded local-amplitude experiment \(\theta\in[-K,K]\).

Put
\[
 A^\circ=\Lambda G_F^{1/2},\qquad B^\circ=F G_F^{-1/2}.
\]
The factor-Gram envelope gives \(\lambda_{\min}(G_F)\geq\underline f>0\), so the two symmetric square roots in this display exist.  Direct multiplication gives
\[
 A^\circ(B^\circ)^{\top}
 =\Lambda G_F^{1/2}G_F^{-1/2}F^{\top}
 =\Lambda F^{\top}
\]
and
\[
 T^{-1}(B^\circ)^{\top}B^\circ
 =G_F^{-1/2}(T^{-1}F^{\top}F)G_F^{-1/2}
 =I_r.
\]
For every row \(i\), the loading-row bound and the upper factor-Gram envelope imply
\[
 \|A^\circ_{i\cdot}\|_2
 \leq \|\Lambda_{i\cdot}\|_2\|G_F^{1/2}\|_{\mathrm{op}}
 \leq \overline\ell\sqrt{\overline f}<C_A.
\]
Likewise, for every row \(t\), the factor-row bound and the lower factor-Gram envelope imply
\[
 \|B^\circ_{t\cdot}\|_2
 \leq \|F_{t\cdot}\|_2\|G_F^{-1/2}\|_{\mathrm{op}}
 \leq \frac{\overline g}{\sqrt{\underline f}}<C_B.
\]
Thus \((A^\circ,B^\circ)\) is feasible, with fixed positive slack in both row-radius restrictions.  In particular, it is feasible for all arrays satisfying the stated envelopes, hence certainly for all sufficiently large \(N,T\).

Let
\[
 I_1=\{i:d_i=1\},\quad I_0=\{i:d_i=0\},\qquad
 J_1=\{t:qvec_t=1\},\quad J_0=\{t:qvec_t=0\}.
\]
The share envelope and the proportional-asymptotics envelope imply that the four cardinalities \(|I_1|,|I_0|,|J_1|,|J_0|\) are respectively of orders \(N,N,T,T\), uniformly along the triangular array.  Write \(P_{\Omega_0}\) for entrywise restriction to \(\Omega_0\), with zeros outside \(\Omega_0\), and put \(L^\circ=\Lambda F^{\top}\).

First observe that the training law contains no treatment signal.  If \((i,t)\in\Omega_0\), then \(d_iqvec_t=0\).  Consequently
\[
 D_{it}=0,\qquad
 H_{it}=\delta(d_i a_i)(qvec_t b_t)=0,\qquad
 Y_{it}=L^\circ_{it}+E_{it}.
\tag{1}
\]
This identity holds for every value of \(\theta\).

We next establish the only rate about the masked fit that will be needed.  Use the feasible normalization from the preceding lemma,
\[
 A^\circ=\Lambda G_F^{1/2},\qquad B^\circ=F G_F^{-1/2},\qquad
 L^\circ=A^\circ(B^\circ)^{\top}.
\tag{2}
\]
Subscripts \(0\) and \(1\) on these factor matrices denote restriction to the corresponding index sets.  The restricted-Gram envelopes and the factor-Gram envelope yield fixed constants \(c_A,c_B>0\) such that, eventually,
\[
 \lambda_{\min}\bigl((A^\circ_0)^{\top}A^\circ_0\bigr)
 \geq c_A N,
 \qquad
 \lambda_{\min}\bigl((B^\circ_0)^{\top}B^\circ_0\bigr)
 \geq c_B T.
\tag{3}
\]
Indeed,
\[
 N^{-1}(A^\circ_0)^{\top}A^\circ_0
 =G_F^{1/2}(N^{-1}\Lambda^{\top}M_d\Lambda)G_F^{1/2}
\]
has smallest eigenvalue at least \(\underline f\,\underline\lambda_0\), while
\[
 T^{-1}(B^\circ_0)^{\top}B^\circ_0
 =G_F^{-1/2}(T^{-1}F^{\top}M_{qvec}F)G_F^{-1/2}
\]
has smallest eigenvalue at least \(\underline f_0/\overline f\).

Let \(\widehat L_M=\widehat A\widehat B^{\top}\) be any global minimizer in the masked fitting class, in particular the lexicographically selected one, and define
\[
 \Delta_L=\widehat L_M-L^\circ,\qquad Z=P_{\Omega_0}E.
\]
Existence follows because the feasible parameter set is nonempty by the preceding lemma, closed, and bounded, and the criterion is continuous.  Comparing the minimizer with the feasible pair in (2), and using (1), gives the basic inequality
\[
 \|P_{\Omega_0}\Delta_L\|_F^2
 \leq 2\langle Z,P_{\Omega_0}\Delta_L\rangle.
\tag{4}
\]
Since \(\operatorname{rank}(\Delta_L)\leq2r\) and deleting the rectangle \(I_1\times J_1\) adds at most another \(2r\) to rank,
\[
 \operatorname{rank}(P_{\Omega_0}\Delta_L)\leq4r.
\tag{5}
\]
For completeness, a one-quarter-net argument on the two Euclidean unit spheres gives
\[
 \|Z\|_{\mathrm{op}}=O_p\bigl(\sigma(\sqrt N+\sqrt T)\bigr).
\tag{6}
\]
To see this directly, for fixed unit vectors \(u,v\), the variable \(u^{\top}Zv\) is centered Gaussian with variance at most \(\sigma^2\); union bounding its Gaussian exponential tail over nets of cardinalities at most \(9^N\) and \(9^T\), and then using the deterministic net approximation for the operator norm, proves (6).  Hölder's inequality for the nuclear and operator norms, followed by (5), now turns (4) into
\[
 \|P_{\Omega_0}\Delta_L\|_F
 \leq4\sqrt r\,\|Z\|_{\mathrm{op}}
 =O_p(\sqrt m),
\tag{7}
\]
where the last equality uses the noise-scale and aspect-ratio envelopes.

We record the factor consequence of (3) and (7), including its derivation.  The complete control-row block \(I_0\times\{1,\ldots,T\}\) is observed.  If \(P_{\widehat B}\) is the orthogonal projector onto the columns of \(\widehat B\), then
\[
 \|A^\circ_0(B^\circ)^{\top}(I-P_{\widehat B})\|_F
 \leq \|P_{\Omega_0}\Delta_L\|_F.
\]
Using the first bound in (3) and dividing by \(\sqrt T\) shows that the sine distance between the column spaces of \(B^\circ\) and \(\widehat B\) is \(O_p(m^{-1/2})\).  Similarly, the complete pre-period block \(\{1,\ldots,N\}\times J_0\), together with the second bound in (3), shows that the sine distance between the column spaces of \(A^\circ\) and \(\widehat A\) is \(O_p(m^{-1/2})\).  Both fitted factor matrices have full column rank with probability tending to one, since otherwise either projection inequality would contradict (3) and (7).  Orthogonal Procrustes alignment, followed by multiplication of the two observed block errors by the inverses of the two Grams in (3), therefore supplies an orthogonal matrix \(R\) for which
\[
 \|\widehat A-A^\circ R\|_F=O_p(1),
 \qquad
 \|\widehat B-B^\circ R\|_F=O_p(1).
\tag{8}
\]
Here is the elementary scaling in the last step.  The normalized sine error is \(O_p(m^{-1/2})\), multiplication by \(\sqrt N\) or \(\sqrt T\) gives an \(O_p(1)\) factor error under proportional asymptotics, and the remaining coefficient error is at most the observed matrix error in (7) divided by the relevant smallest singular value, which is of order \(\sqrt m\) by (3).  Thus (8) follows without a rate theorem external to this proof.

The deterministic row-radius slack proved in the preceding lemma makes the constraints asymptotically inactive.  We justify this rather than assume it.  Conditional least squares for any row uses at least a fixed fraction of the opposite panel dimension by the share envelope and (3).  Decompose its score into the score at \((A^\circ R,B^\circ R)\) and the remainder in (8).  Gaussian exponential tails and a union bound over \(O(m)\) rows give
\[
 \max_i\|\widehat A_{i\cdot}-(A^\circ R)_{i\cdot}\|_2
 +\max_t\|\widehat B_{t\cdot}-(B^\circ R)_{t\cdot}\|_2
 =O_p\!\left(\sqrt{\frac{\log m}{m}}+\frac1{\sqrt m}\right)=o_p(1).
\tag{9}
\]
For example, the fixed part of an \(A\)-row score is Gaussian with covariance bounded by a constant times \(T\), so its maximum divided by a Gram of order \(T\) is \(O_p(\sqrt{\log m/m})\); the remainder is bounded by \(\|E_{i\cdot}\|_2\|\widehat B-B^\circ R\|_F/T=O_p(m^{-1/2})\), uniformly, using (8) and the same Gaussian union bound.  The transposed calculation gives the \(B\)-row bound.  Since the two true row bounds are separated from \(C_A,C_B\) by fixed positive constants, (9) proves inactivity with probability tending to one, uniformly over all global minimizers.

On this event, the usual unconstrained rank-\(r\) normal equations are valid.  The normalization of \(\widehat B\) causes no restriction here: every sufficiently small rank-\(r\) matrix perturbation can be renormalized by an invertible right change of coordinates, and (9) keeps the resulting factorization inside both row-radius bounds.  Hence
\[
 \widehat A_1
 =Y_{10}\widehat B_0(\widehat B_0^{\top}\widehat B_0)^{-1},
 \qquad
 \widehat B_1
 =Y_{01}^{\top}\widehat A_0(\widehat A_0^{\top}\widehat A_0)^{-1},
\tag{10}
\]
where \(Y_{10}=Y_{I_1,J_0}\) and \(Y_{01}=Y_{I_0,J_1}\).  Equations (3) and (8) also imply
\[
 \| (\widehat B_0^{\top}\widehat B_0)^{-1}\|_{\mathrm{op}}=O_p(T^{-1}),
 \qquad
 \| (\widehat A_0^{\top}\widehat A_0)^{-1}\|_{\mathrm{op}}=O_p(N^{-1}).
\tag{11}
\]

Exact orthogonality now produces the sharper aggregate rate.  By left-support orthogonality,
\[
 n_1^{-1}\mathbf 1_{I_1}^{\top}A^\circ_1
 =n_1^{-1}d^{\top}\Lambda G_F^{1/2}=0.
\tag{12}
\]
Thus, with \(\overline E_{10}=n_1^{-1}\mathbf 1_{I_1}^{\top}E_{10}\), the first equation in (10) gives
\[
 n_1^{-1}\mathbf 1_{I_1}^{\top}\widehat A_1
 =\overline E_{10}\widehat B_0(\widehat B_0^{\top}\widehat B_0)^{-1}.
\tag{13}
\]
The vector \(\overline E_{10}B^\circ_0R\) is centered Gaussian with covariance
\[
 \frac{\sigma^2}{n_1}R^{\top}(B^\circ_0)^{\top}B^\circ_0R=O(1),
\]
while \(\|\overline E_{10}\|_2=O_p(1)\) and \(\|\widehat B_0-B^\circ_0R\|_F=O_p(1)\) by (8).  No independence is needed for the latter product.  Combining these facts with (11) proves
\[
 \left\|n_1^{-1}\mathbf 1_{I_1}^{\top}\widehat A_1\right\|_2=O_p(T^{-1}).
\tag{14}
\]
The right-support orthogonality similarly gives
\[
 t_1^{-1}\mathbf 1_{J_1}^{\top}B^\circ_1
 =t_1^{-1}qvec^{\top}F G_F^{-1/2}=0.
\tag{15}
\]
Applying the transposed argument to the second equation in (10) yields
\[
 \left\|t_1^{-1}\mathbf 1_{J_1}^{\top}\widehat B_1\right\|_2=O_p(N^{-1}).
\tag{16}
\]
Because the mean of a rank-\(r\) product over a rectangle factors into the product of its two factor means, (14)--(16) imply
\[
 \frac1{n_1t_1}\sum_{i\in I_1}\sum_{t\in J_1}\widehat L_{M,it}
 =\left(n_1^{-1}\mathbf 1_{I_1}^{\top}\widehat A_1\right)
   \left(t_1^{-1}\mathbf 1_{J_1}^{\top}\widehat B_1\right)^{\top}
 =O_p((NT)^{-1})
 =o_p((n_1t_1)^{-1/2}).
\tag{17}
\]

It remains to verify studentization.  Let \(R_M=\sum_{(i,t)\in\Omega_0}(Y_{it}-\widehat L_{M,it})^2\).  From (4)--(7), (5), and the same nuclear-norm inequality,
\[
 |R_M-\|Z\|_F^2|=O_p(m).
\tag{18}
\]
The share envelope gives \(|\Omega_0|=NT-n_1t_1\asymp NT\), whereas fixed \(r\) gives \(r(N+T-r)=O(m)\).  Therefore \(\nu_M>0\) eventually and \(\nu_M/|\Omega_0|\to1\).  Moreover, Gaussianity gives
\[
 \mathbb E\!\left[\frac{\|Z\|_F^2}{\sigma^2|\Omega_0|}\right]=1,
 \qquad
 \operatorname{Var}\!\left(\frac{\|Z\|_F^2}{\sigma^2|\Omega_0|}\right)=\frac2{|\Omega_0|}\to0.
\]
Equation (18), divided by \(\nu_M\), consequently proves
\[
 \widehat\sigma_M^2\xrightarrow{p}\sigma^2,
 \qquad
 \widehat\sigma_M\xrightarrow{p}\sigma,
\tag{19}
\]
where the second conclusion uses \(\sigma\geq\underline\sigma>0\).

Finally, exact orthogonality gives an exact expression for the treated-post mean of the data.  Namely,
\[
 \frac1{n_1t_1}\sum_{i\in I_1,t\in J_1}L^\circ_{it}=0
\]
by either (12) or (15), and the definitions of the supported moments give
\[
 \frac1{n_1t_1}\sum_{i\in I_1,t\in J_1}H_{it}
 =\delta\mu_{a,N}\mu_{b,T}.
\]
Hence, writing \(\overline E_{11}=(n_1t_1)^{-1}\sum_{i\in I_1,t\in J_1}E_{it}\),
\[
 \widehat{\operatorname{ATT}}_M-\operatorname{ATT}_{NT}
 =\overline E_{11}
 -\frac1{n_1t_1}\sum_{i\in I_1,t\in J_1}\widehat L_{M,it}.
\tag{20}
\]
The first term satisfies \(\sqrt{n_1t_1}\,\overline E_{11}/\sigma\sim\mathcal N(0,1)\) exactly.  Equations (17), (19), and (20), followed by Slutsky's argument, prove
\[
 \frac{\sqrt{n_1t_1}(\widehat{\operatorname{ATT}}_M-\operatorname{ATT}_{NT})}{\widehat\sigma_M}
 \Rightarrow\mathcal N(0,1).
\tag{21}
\]
All random quantities on the right side of (20), including the masked fit and its residual variance, have a finite-sample law independent of \(\theta\) by (1); the \(\theta\)-dependent treated-post mean has been removed exactly through \(\operatorname{ATT}_{NT}\).  Thus every remainder bound above is the same for every \(\theta\in[-K,K]\), and (17), (19), and (21) hold uniformly on that compact interval.  Taking the probability of the event that the absolute value in (21) is at most \(z_{1-\alpha/2}\), and using continuity of the standard-normal distribution, gives
\[
 \inf_{\theta\in[-K,K]}
 \Pr\{\operatorname{ATT}_{NT}\in\mathrm{CI}_M\}\longrightarrow1-\alpha,
\]
as claimed.

proposed.statement: Uniformly over \(\theta\in[-K,K]\), \(\sqrt{n_1t_1}(\widehat{\operatorname{ATT}}_M-\operatorname{ATT}_{NT})/\widehat\sigma_M\Rightarrow\mathcal N(0,1)\), \(\widehat\sigma_M\xrightarrow{p}\sigma\), and \(\inf_{\theta\in[-K,K]}\Pr\{\operatorname{ATT}_{NT}\in\mathrm{CI}_M\}\to1-\alpha\). In addition, \((n_1t_1)^{-1}\sum_{i:d_i=1}\sum_{t:qvec_t=1}\widehat L_{M,it}=o_p((n_1t_1)^{-1/2})\) uniformly.
proposed.justification: As an internal control, masking removes the heterogeneous treatment factor from every training cell, so uniformity spans the bounded absorption transition.
proposed.gap: Bai and Ng (2021) give pointwise block-imputation normality, not this compact-amplitude result paired with full-sample absorption.
proposed.consumer: It supplies an internal benchmark showing that the full-sample failure is caused by fitting the treated-post spike rather than by the Gaussian oracle experiment itself.

proposed_core_edits.reason: The proof uses the proportional rectangular asymptotic envelope declared by the panel topic. Adding the already-frozen aspect-ratio assumption repairs the theorem's dependency metadata without changing its claim.
